title: Salted caramel sauce
summary: A glossy, buttery salted caramel made with allulose, which browns like sugar and stays smooth instead of recrystallising.
steps: Put the allulose and water in a heavy, light-coloured saucepan so you can see the colour change. Stir once to wet it, then cook over medium-low heat without stirring.

Let it bubble until it turns a deep amber, 6–10 minutes. Allulose browns faster and at a lower temperature than sugar, so stay with it and swirl the pan rather than stirring; pull it off the heat the moment it smells toasty.
Off the heat, whisk in the butter a piece at a time. It will foam.
Slowly pour in the warm cream, whisking; stand back, as it sputters.
Return to low heat and simmer 2–3 minutes, whisking, until smooth and slightly thickened. Stir in the salt and vanilla.
Cool 20 minutes before using; it thickens as it cools. Sprinkle a few flakes of sea salt over the sauce as you serve it. Refrigerate up to 2 weeks and warm gently to loosen.
dairy_free_notes: With coconut cream the sauce is a little thinner and tastes faintly of coconut; simmer it a minute longer to thicken.
tips: Erythritol does not caramelise and crystallises as it cools, so it is not a substitute here.
Add the salt in stages and taste: the Breton style is noticeably salty.

origin.history: Brittany has long been known for salted butter, and caramel made with it is a regional speciality. The modern fame of salted-butter caramel is often credited to the Quiberon confectioner Henri Le Roux, whose salted-butter caramels of the 1970s were widely copied. The salty-sweet sauce has since spread far beyond France.
